sections.heading: Page 3
paragraphs: Internal Audit Final Report
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The Department of Building Inspection (DBI) affirms its mission to “protect our community by
ensuring code- compliant construction, building safety, resilience, and habitability, and by
supporting economic development in San Francisco.” This mission is the cornerstone of the
department’s primary role and focus: enforcing building and related codes to ensure the safety
of San Francisco’s built environment.
In April 2020, following a public integrity scandal in the city that involved individuals from several
city departments and led to the resignation of DBI’s former director Tom Hui in early 2020, Patrick
O’Riordan was promoted to lead the department. He oversaw a set of comprehensive reforms
to strengthen the public integrity of DBI’s services and operations and to begin restoring public
trust.
Following the department’s reforms initiative, the Controller’s Office conducted a public integrity
review and issued a report in September 2021 that outlined eight recommendations “to improve
or strengthen city systems, policies, procedures, internal controls and transparency.” Many of
the Controller’s recommendations aligned with DBI’s ongoing reform initiatives and efforts
already in progress at the department. In August 2024, the Controller’s Office issued a follow-up
report confirming that the Controller Office’s eight recommended actions for DBI had been
“implemented and closed.”
As part of its effort to address the previous lapses, DBI launched an internal audit of properties
associated with federally convicted engineer Rodrigo Santos and former senior building
inspector Bernard Curran to determine whether the construction work they oversaw posed any
serious life-safety concerns. The department identified the properties to be included in the audit,
established a methodology for reviewing the properties, conduct ed the reviews and then sent
flagged non-compliant properties to its code-enforcement division for further action. This work
took more than four years to complete.
While DBI identified 136 properties with code violations, the audit did not uncover any seri ous
life-safety conditions. The department is working with the Board of Supervisors and the Planning

Department to pass an ordinance to streamline the process for audited properties with violations.
This ordinance would allow owners to abate the violations and legalize any non- compliant
conditions that are not a life- safety hazard. Moving forward, DBI will address any additional
noncompliant conditions associated with these two individuals through its regular code-
enforcement process.
BACKGROUND
In March 2018, DBI discovered irregularities in payments made to the department by Rodrigo
Santos, a San Francisco based engineer and former president of the city’s Building Inspection
Commission, and notified the Controller’s Office. After an investigation, the City Attorney brought
a lawsuit against Rodrigo Santos and others for fraud related to construction projects in San
Francisco. The lawsuit included charges that Santos has performed excavation work that
exceeded the scope of permitted work, which can pose a serious safety hazard, and that he had
fraudulently certified some special inspections for certain projects. In May 2020, the U.S.
Attorney’s office charged Mr. Santos with fraud related to the irregular payments and later filed
additional criminal charges against him in 2021 alleging that Santos had bribed Bernard Curran,
a senior building inspector at DBI.
In 2021, DBI took immediate action to address the alleged misconduct by former Senior Building
Inspector Bernard Curran by placing him on administrative leave and launching an investigation
into his work. In August 2021, the U.S. Attorney’s office filed criminal charges against Mr. Curran,
charging him with accepting bribes , providing preferential treatment for Mr. S antos and his
clients, and approving projects that had not completed the work on the approved permit.
In 2022, Curran pleaded guilty to two counts of accepting illegal gratuities under Title 18, United
States Code, Section 666(a)(1)(B). Santos pleaded guilty to multiple counts, including honest
services wire fraud under Title 18, United States Code, Section 1343, for his role in the scheme.
Both men served time in prison.
DBI launched the internal audit reviewing their work in fall 2021, and the audit was completed
earlier this year.

sections.heading: Page 5
paragraphs: Internal Audit Final Report
SCOPE
In consultation with the City Attorney’s Office, DBI determined that , due to the criminal
convictions of Rodrigo Santos and Bernie Curran, it was necessary to review properties
associated with them to fulfill the department’s mission of ensuring code-compliant construction
and building safety. This building review began in fall 2021 as the department’s internal audit
and included 5,445 properties:
• All 2,542 properties linked to Rodrigo Santos.
• All 3,021 properties at which former Senior Building Inspector Bernard Curran performed
same-day inspections.
In consultation with the City Attorney’s Office, DBI limited the scope of the audit related to Mr.
Curran to same- day inspections. The department’s inspections division is structured as an
assignment system , and the protocol states that inspectors can only perform same -day
inspections (that they schedule themselves) under certain conditions, such as for an urgent
condition or for efficiency if an inspector is already at a property or nearby.
DBI’s Building Inspection Division (BID) divides San Francisco into 18 inspection districts. One
building inspector is assigned to each district and reports to one of BID ’s six senior building
inspectors. According to the division’s policies and procedures, the district inspector should be
assigned to all inspections in his/her district. If the district inspector cannot perform the
inspection, the senior building inspector will assign the inspection to someone else based on an
assignment matrix that typically assigns the inspection to a floating inspector and has further
protocols for assignment as necessary.
Normally, inspections are scheduled in advance. Same- day inspections are typically reserved
for urgent situations and are not common practice. However, the investigation revealed that Mr.
Curran had conducted a large number of same -day inspections, and the federal complaint
detailed how Mr. Curran abused and manipulated the inspections process so that he could
approve projects improperly or without visiting the property. Because of this, the audit focused
more narrowly on Curran’s same-day activities while reviewing all projects linked to Santos.

The audit team reviewed properties in this order:
• Tier 1 (119 properties): Reviewed first because these addresses involved both Curran
and Santos. When both individuals worked on the same project, the risk of potential
misconduct was considered highest.
• Tier 2 (158 properties): Reviewed next. These properties involved either Curran or
Santos and were located in a Slope Protection Area, which carries stricter requirements
due to potential life-safety risks.
• Tier 3 (5,168 properties): Reviewed last. These were the remaining properties
associated with either Curran or Santos, but not located in a Slope Protection Area and
thus considered lower risk.
This tiered approach allowed DBI to focus audit resources where issues were most likely to
occur.

METHODOLOGY
The audit review team used a phased approach to review 5,445 properties. The team developed
a custom audit tool, applied defined criteria to determine follow -up actions, and used both full
and sample audits to manage the high volume of Tier 3 properties.
The diagram below summarizes DBI’s three-phase audit methodology. The process begins with
initial property screening using the audit app, continues with a flag-based review, and concludes
with follow-up actions, including enforcement when necessary.
This flowchart of our three- phase process highlights the decision points and outcomes that
guided how DBI reviewed each property:
DBI’s Three-Phase Internal Audit Process
Phase 1 – Audit App Review
DBI launched the review process by building a custom online screening tool using Oracle APEX,
referred to as the “audit app.” This tool allowed reviewers to evaluate each property
systematically by answering 15 standardized questions based on defined audit criteria. (See
Appendix B for the full list of questions).

To complete their assessments, reviewers consulted:
• Permit and inspection records in DBI’s Permit Tracking System (PTS).
• Approved construction plans.
• Google Street View for exterior views and construction timelines.
• Redfin and Zillow for interior views and listing history.
Reviewers entered their findings directly into the audit app, which compiled and aggregated
responses to support broader analysis and determine next steps.
Based on this review, the team placed each property into one of two categories:
1. Review Clear / No Follow-Up Required
2. Reviewed / Follow-Up Required

Phase 2 – Additional Review
In the second phase of the audit, DBI reviewed each property flagged during Phase 1 to
determine the appropriate follow-up action. The audit team used defined criteria to assign one
of three outcomes: no flag, yellow flag, or red flag.

• No Flag:
o DBI completed additional review and found no issues.
o The audit team cleared the property from the audit.
• Yellow Flag:
o Reviewers identified minor administrative issues, typically expired permits. DBI
flagged these properties for follow-up outreach to the property owner.
o In most cases, the expired permits were associated with projects requiring a
Certificate of Final Completion (CFC).
• Red Flag:
o Reviewers confirmed more serious issues that required formal enforcement.
DBI referred these properties to the Com plaint Investigation Team (CIT) for
follow-up. The CIT team scheduled a site inspection and prepared a potential
Notice of Violation (NOV). The audit team assigned red flags in cases where
they identified:
 Construction that exceeded the scope of the approved permit.
 Missing required inspections.
 Exterior changes that did not match approved plans.
 Incomplete or non-finaled trade permits.
DBI closed each red- flagged property from the audit once staff created a complaint in the
Permit / Complaint Tracking System.
Phase 3 – Follow-Up Action and Close Out
In the third phase, DBI completed follow -up actions for flagged properties and formally closed
them from the audit. The audit team used different procedures depending on whether a property
received a yellow or red flag.
Yellow Flag
DBI identified minor administrative issues, primarily expired permits, at yellow -flagged
properties. Staff mailed formal notices to property owners outlining the steps required to

sections.heading: Page 10
paragraphs: Internal Audit Final Report
resolve the issue, such as renewing the expired permit. Once DBI sent the notice, the
audit team cleared the property from the audit.
Red Flag
For red -flagged properties, DBI took immediate enforcement steps. The audit team
referred each property to the Complaint Investigation Team (CIT), who opened a formal
complaint in the Complaint Tracking System, scheduled a site inspection, and evaluated
whether to issue a Notice of Violation (NOV). DBI cleared each red-flagged property from
the audit after initiating the complaint in CTS. CIT continues to monitor these properties
through ongoing enforcement using the Complaint Tracking System.
Tier 3: Audit Strategies
After completing the Tier 1 and Tier 2 reviews, DBI faced 5,168 remaining Tier 3 properties.
Conducting a full audit of every property would have required several years. To address this
volume efficiently, the audit team divided Tier 3 properties into two categories:
1. Properties that met defined criteria for a full audit review.
2. Remaining properties selected for a representative sample audit.
Tier 3: Full Review
After completing the Tier 1 and 2 reviews, DBI turned to the remaining 5,168 Tier 3 properties.
A full audit of every Tier 3 property would have required several years. To focus efforts on the
highest risk cases, the audit team identified specific criteria to determine which properties
warranted a complete review.

criteria:

Tier 3: Representative Sample Audit
After completing full reviews for 3,014 Tier 3 properties, DBI used a representative sample audit
to evaluate the remaining 1,973 properties. This approach allowed the audit team to efficiently
evaluate lower risk properties while still identifying any red flags or patterns that might warrant
concern.
To implement this strategy, the audit team:
• Grouped the 1,973 properties into five categories based on permit and inspection
characteristics.
• Conducted full reviews on a sample of at least 15% of properties from each group. Actual
sample rates ranged from 16.72% to 32.10%.
• Cleared all remaining properties within a group only if the reviewed sample set showed
no major issues.

Erroneous Inclusion
During the review process, the audit team discovered 194 properties that were incorrectly
included in the Tier 3 audit. These entries appeared due to applicant names resembling those
of Rodrigo Santos, but had no actual association with him. After confirming the error, the team
cleared all 194 properties from the audit.
FINDINGS
DBI audited 5,445 properties using a three-phase process and a risk-based strategy to
prioritize cases needing closer review. The pie chart below illustrates the overall audit
outcomes, showing the proportion of properties cleared versus those flagged for further review:

sections.heading: Page 14
paragraphs: Internal Audit Final Report
• 5,151 properties (94.6%) were cleared with no major issues identified.
• 294 properties (5.4%) were flagged for additional review or follow -up during the initial
audit phase.
These results demonstrate the audit team’s ability to efficiently clear compliant properties while
identifying those that need closer scrutiny.
Of the 294 flagged properties:
• 182 properties received red flags due to potential code violations. DBI referred these
cases to the code enforcement division for further investigation and potential issuance of
a Notice of Violation (NOV). An NOV was issued if staff verif ied the non -compliant
condition after an inspection.
• 111 properties were flagged yellow due to expired permits. DBI sent letters to these
property owners advising them to contact the department about next steps.
• 1 property was cleared after additional review confirmed no violation.
Following further investigation, 177 of the 182 red- flagged properties led to open complaints.
The remaining five were resolved without formal complaints after staff obtained clarifying
information.
To date:
• 136 of 177 complaints resulted in a Notice of Violation.
• The remaining 41 properties are still under investigation by the code enforcement division
due to limited access, owner nonresponse, or other delays. These complaints will remain
open until resolved.
For more details on flagged properties and audit notes, see Appendix C.

sections.heading: Page 15
paragraphs: Internal Audit Final Report
CONCLUSION
DBI’s mission statement affirms that the department “protects our community by ensuring code-
compliant construction, building safety, resilience, and habitability, and by supporting economic
development in San Francisco.” In 2020, details emerged about a public integrity scandal
involving individuals from several city departments that led to the resignations of multiple
department heads as well as criminal charges and convictions of several individuals. Among
those convicted were engineer Rodrigo Santos and former senior building inspector Bernard
Curran.
To determine whether the construction work they oversaw posed any serious life safety
concerns, the department ide ntified more than five thousand properties to include in the audit .
Over the next four years, DBI completed the reviews and referred flagged non- compliant
properties to the its code enforcement division for further action.
While the department found 1 36 properties with code violations, the audit did not uncover any
serious life safety conditions. The department is working with the Board of Supervisors and the
Planning Department to pass an ordinance to streamline the process for properties in the audit
that received violations to abate the violations and legalize any non- compliant conditions that
are not a life-safety hazard.
The department remains committed to transparency, accountability, and continued vigilance in
upholding public trust. DBI has implemented multiple safeguards through its reform initiative to
prevent these types of abuses in the future. Moving forward, t he department will address any
additional noncompliant conditions associated with these two individuals through its regular
code-enforcement process.
